question: What is considered the gold standard for assessing a patient's pain?
explanation: Pain is entirely subjective, meaning the patient's own description is the most reliable and accurate indicator of their experience. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do nurses refer to pain as the 'fifth vital sign'?

options.A: It directly calculates the exact heart rate of the patient.
options.B: It can be measured using an automated cuff machine.
options.C: It must be checked and recorded alongside standard vital signs.
options.D: It is only relevant during surgical procedures.

explanation: Calling pain the fifth vital sign reminds us to assess and document it just as regularly as temperature or blood pressure. Great job keeping your clinical habits sharp! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h1)

question: A patient complains of a burning, shooting pain down their leg from a pinched nerve. What kind of pain is this?
explanation: When the nervous system itself is damaged, it often causes burning, tingling, or shooting sensations. That's classic neuropathic pain! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is the main difference between acute and chronic pain?

options.A: Acute pain is tied to recent tissue injury and resolves with healing, while chronic pain lasts long past the normal healing period.
options.B: Acute pain can be measured with scales, but chronic pain cannot be measured.
options.C: Acute pain requires no medical treatment, whereas chronic pain requires surgery.
options.D: Acute pain only affects internal organs, while chronic pain only affects the skin and muscles.

explanation: Think of acute pain as a sudden alarm bell that stops when healing happens, while chronic pain sticks around long after the injury has healed. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h2)

question: In the pain assessment mnemonic OPQRSTUV, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?
explanation: The letter Q refers to quality, prompting the nurse to ask what the pain actually feels like to the patient. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h3)

question: When a nurse asks a patient, 'What makes your stomach pain better or worse?', what are they checking?
explanation: Spot on! Asking what triggers or relieves the discomfort helps you figure out the provoking (starting) and palliating (soothing) factors. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which pain scale uses cartoon faces ranging from a happy smile to a crying face?
explanation: The Wong-Baker FACES scale uses friendly facial drawings, making it super helpful for children or patients who struggle to use numbers. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which of these is a dangerous trap nurses should avoid when assessing patient pain?

options.A: Asking about the location of the discomfort
options.B: Believing that self-report is always the best method
options.C: Assuming a sleeping patient is completely free of pain
options.D: Using a 0-10 scale for adults with normal cognition

explanation: Never assume sleep means zero pain! Exhaustion can cause patients to drift off even when they are hurting badly. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why must nurses be careful when evaluating pain in older adult patients?

options.A: Older adults do not experience acute nociceptive pain.
options.B: Older adults always report pain at a much higher intensity than young adults.
options.C: Standard rating scales cannot be understood by anyone over age sixty-five.
options.D: Pain should never be assumed to be a normal, expected part of aging.

explanation: Never brush off pain just because someone is elderly. Assuming it's 'just old age' leads to missing treatable problems! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h5)

question: A patient with advanced dementia makes a pain face, holds their tummy, and has a fast heart rate, but says they have no pain. What should you do?

options.A: Discharge the patient because they cannot feel pain.
options.B: Ignore the physical signs since the verbal denial overrides them.
options.C: Treat these non-verbal behavioral signs as reliable indicators of pain.
options.D: Wait until the patient is able to provide a clear numeric score.

explanation: When dementia makes talking difficult, body language tells the real story. Trust those physical cues! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h5)

question: When is the best time to check back on a patient after giving them oral pain medication?
explanation: Oral meds usually take 30 to 60 minutes to kick in. That's your window to return and see if the drug is doing its job! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why is writing down complete notes about pain care so important for nurses?

options.A: It replaces the need to talk directly with the patient.
options.B: It is only required for legal protection during lawsuits.
options.C: It ensures safe continuity of care and evaluates if treatment worked.
options.D: It allows the hospital to bill insurance companies faster.

explanation: Clear notes help the whole healthcare team see what worked, keep the patient safe, and coordinate the next steps smoothly. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T5#GNS321_U4_T5_h6)
